description.en: The barbell resistance band hip thrust adds resistance bands to a standard barbell hip thrust. The bands attach to the bar and anchor low, providing accommodating resistance that increases at the top of the lift where the glutes are most active. It builds glute size with progressive load.

en: Set up with upper back against a bench, barbell across your hips.
Attach resistance bands to each end of the bar and anchor them to a low point.
Plant your feet flat on the floor with knees bent.
Brace your core and pin your shoulders to the bench.
Drive your hips up by squeezing your glutes hard.
The band tension will increase as you lift toward lockout.
Continue lifting until your hips are fully extended.
Lower your hips back down with control.
Combines barbell load with accommodating band resistance
Heaviest glute load at lockout
Forces strong glute squeeze
Builds glute size with progressive overload
Trains the glutes through their strongest range
Useful for breaking through hip thrust plateaus

description.en: The barbell standing ab rollout uses a barbell with weight plates rolling on the floor like an ab wheel. From a standing position, you bend forward and roll the bar away from your feet, then pull it back. The standing position is significantly harder than the kneeling rollout and demands extreme core and lat strength.

en: Load a barbell with weight plates that allow the bar to roll smoothly.
Stand facing the bar with feet hip-width apart.
Bend forward and grip the bar with both hands shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core hard and engage your lats.
Roll the bar forward away from your feet, lowering your body toward the floor.
Continue rolling out until you reach a near-horizontal position.
Engage your abs and lats hard to roll the bar back toward your feet.
Pull yourself back up to the standing position.
Extreme core strength demand
Builds total core and lat strength
Advanced ab rollout variation
Useful for breaking through ab plateaus
Strong functional carryover
Develops anti-extension core strength

description.en: The barbell sumo deadlift from blocks raises the starting position of the sumo deadlift by setting the plates on stacked blocks or platforms. The shorter range lets you handle more weight, building lockout strength in the sumo position. It is excellent for sumo lifters working through sticking points.

en: Stack blocks or platforms under each plate to raise the bar.
Set the bar height so the plates rest just below or above your knees.
Stand over the bar with a wide sumo stance, toes turned out.
Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar with hands inside your legs.
Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and engage your lats.
Drive through your feet and push the floor away to stand up.
Lock out at the top with hips fully extended.
Lower the bar back to the blocks with control.
Allows heavier loads than full sumo deadlifts
Builds lockout strength in sumo position
Reduces stress on the lower back
Excellent accessory for competition sumo deadlift
Useful for working through sumo sticking points
Heavy upper back overload

description.en: The battling ropes alternate arms squat combines battle rope waves with an isometric squat hold. The lifter holds a low squat while alternating arm waves with the ropes. The combo is a brutal full body conditioning move that hits the legs, shoulders, and core.

en: Anchor battle ropes to a sturdy point.
Grip one rope end in each hand.
Step back to take some slack out of the ropes.
Drop into a parallel squat and hold it.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Begin alternating arm waves driving the ropes up and down.
Maintain the squat hold for the duration.
Continue the alternating waves at speed.
Brutal full body finisher
Builds shoulder endurance
Trains cardio capacity
Builds leg endurance
Strong conditioning move
Builds core stability

description.en: The bottle weighted halo is a halo style shoulder mobility move performed with a weighted bottle or jug instead of a kettlebell. The bottle circles around the head to mobilize the shoulders and warm up the upper body for training.

en: Stand tall holding a weighted bottle in both hands at chest level.
Set your feet at hip-width and brace your core.
Grip the bottle by the handle and the bottom.
Begin circling the bottle around your head in a halo motion.
Keep the bottle close to your head as it travels around.
Move slowly and control the bottle through the full path.
Complete several halos in one direction.
Reverse the direction and circle the other way.
Mobilizes the shoulders
Builds shoulder strength
No KB or DB required
Useful warm-up move
Easy to scale at home
Travel-friendly setup

description.en: The bottle weighted reverse grip concentration curl uses a water bottle as a substitute weight for a reverse grip concentration curl. The lifter sits and curls with palms down, bracing the elbow on the inner thigh. It is a useful home brachialis builder.

en: Sit on a bench with the feet wide apart.
Hold a filled water bottle in one hand with a reverse grip.
Brace the back of the working arm against the inner thigh.
Place the other hand on the opposite knee.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Curl the bottle up toward the shoulder.
Squeeze the brachialis hard at the top.
Lower with control. Finish then switch sides.
Trains the brachialis
Builds the forearms
Strong home option
Useful for arm size
No weights needed

description.en: The cable bent over row is a horizontal pulling exercise performed at a low cable pulley while hinged forward at the hips. The cable provides constant tension throughout the entire range of motion, making it an effective mid-back builder with better tension management than free-weight rows. It is an excellent variation for high-rep hypertrophy work.

en: Attach a straight bar or two D-handles to a low cable pulley.
Stand facing the cable machine with feet hip-width apart. Grip the attachment.
Step back, then hinge forward at the hips until your torso is at roughly 45 degrees from horizontal.
Let your arms hang fully extended with the cable under tension. Brace your core and lock in your back angle.
Row the attachment to your lower chest or upper abdomen by driving your elbows up and back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Pause briefly.
Slowly extend your arms back to the start position. Maintain cable tension and your torso angle throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Constant cable tension throughout the entire range
Excellent for high-rep hypertrophy back work
Multiple attachment options for different stimuli
Easy to load progressively in small increments
Builds the lats, mid-traps, rhomboids, and rear delts
Easier to maintain strict form than free-weight rows

description.en: The cable bent over row with rope attachment is a low cable row done in a hinged stance. The lifter grips the rope, hinges forward, and rows the rope to the lower ribs. The rope grip allows the elbows to flare and trains the upper back well.

en: Attach a rope to a low cable pulley.
Stand facing the cable with the feet hip width apart.
Grip the rope ends with a neutral grip.
Hinge at the hips until the torso is at a forty five degree angle.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Pull the rope toward the lower ribs.
Flare the elbows out as the rope reaches the body.
Lower with control to the start.
Trains the upper back
Strong rope row
Constant cable tension
Builds the lats
Useful back builder
Trains the rear delts

description.en: The cable front seated row is performed sitting facing a low cable pulley with feet braced and a v-handle or wide bar attached. Pulling the handle to the lower chest with elbows tucked builds back thickness and lat strength. The seated position eliminates lower back stress while the cable provides constant tension.

en: Sit at a low cable row station with feet braced on the platform.
Grip a v-handle or close grip attachment with both hands.
Sit tall with chest up and arms extended forward.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Row the handle to your lower chest by driving your elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Slowly extend your arms back to the starting position.
Maintain an upright torso throughout. Avoid rocking back and forth.
Builds back thickness
Constant cable tension through the range
Eliminates lower back stress
Strong lat and rhomboid engagement
Foundation rowing movement
Easy to load progressively

description.en: The cable Pallof press with glute bridge combines two stability movements into one combo. While holding a glute bridge with hips lifted, you press a cable handle straight out from the chest while resisting the lateral pull. The combo trains the glutes and core simultaneously.

en: Set a cable to chest height when lying down with a single handle.
Lie on your back perpendicular to the cable station.
Grip the handle with both hands at your chest.
Plant your feet flat on the floor with knees bent.
Drive your hips up into a glute bridge.
Brace your core hard against the lateral pull of the cable.
While holding the glute bridge, press the handle straight up over your chest.
Bring the handle back to your chest. Continue pressing while holding the bridge. Switch sides.
Combines glute and core training
Strong anti-rotation core demand
Builds glute endurance
Time-efficient compound combo
Useful for athletes who need core stability
Develops total body integration

description.en: The cable upper row uses a high cable pulley to perform a rowing motion where you pull toward your upper chest or face. It emphasizes the rear deltoids, upper trapezius, and rhomboids more than horizontal or low-cable rows.

en: Set a cable to a high position. Attach a rope or straight bar handle.
Stand or sit facing the cable. Grip the handle.
Start with arms extended toward the high cable.
Row the handle toward your face or upper chest by pulling your elbows back.
Squeeze your upper back and rear delts.
Slowly extend back to start.
Keep upright posture throughout.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Targets the upper back, rear delts, and traps
High cable angle provides unique stimulus
Constant cable tension
Easy to load progressively
Similar to face pull but with rowing path
Builds posture and shoulder balance

description.en: The cross body punch in squat position is a conditioning move that holds a low squat while throwing cross body punches. The squat hold loads the legs while the punches train the obliques. It is a useful boxing style cardio drill.

en: Stand with the feet wider than shoulder width.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Lower into a low squat hold.
Make fists and bring the hands up to the chin.
Throw a cross body punch with one arm.
Twist the torso toward the punching arm.
Return the hand to the chin.
Alternate sides at a steady pace.
Burns calories
Trains the obliques
Builds leg endurance
Strong cardio drill
Boxing style move
Useful for conditioning

description.en: The cross body twisting crunch is a classic oblique crunch where the lifter brings the elbow across the body to the opposite knee. The rotation hits the obliques hard while the curl up trains the rectus abdominis. It is a simple no-equipment ab move.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Place the hands lightly behind the head with elbows out wide.
Brace your core and lift the shoulders off the floor.
Twist the torso to bring one elbow across to the opposite knee.
At the same time lift that knee up to meet the elbow.
Squeeze the obliques hard at the top.
Lower back to the start with control.
Alternate sides each rep.
Strong oblique builder
No equipment needed
Trains rotational core
Builds the rectus abdominis
Easy to do anywhere
Useful core finisher

description.en: The double leg butt kick is a cardio drill where you run in place and rapidly kick both heels alternately toward your glutes. It activates the hamstrings, builds running mechanics, and provides effective cardiovascular conditioning. It is a standard warm-up drill for runners and athletes.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Bend your arms at 90 degrees at your sides.
Begin running in place by quickly kicking your right heel up toward your right glute.
As your right foot returns, kick your left heel up toward your left glute.
Continue alternating rapidly. Aim to bring your heels to your glutes (or as close as your flexibility allows).
Pump your arms in opposition to your legs.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Land softly.
Keep your torso upright — do not lean forward.
Perform for 20 to 45 seconds per set.
Activates the hamstrings dynamically
Excellent warm-up for running
Builds hamstring endurance
Improves running mechanics
No equipment needed
Raises heart rate quickly

description.en: The dumbbell curtsey lunge is a lunge variation where you step the back leg behind and across the body (like a curtsey) instead of straight back. The crossover position shifts emphasis to the gluteus medius and adductors of the front leg, making it one of the best exercises for upper glute development.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Step your right foot back and across behind your left leg, like a curtsey.
Lower your hips down by bending both knees. Your right knee should approach the floor.
Keep your front (left) foot flat. Your torso stays upright.
Drive through your front foot to return to standing.
Repeat with the other side — left foot crosses behind right.
Continue alternating for the desired number of reps.
Use moderate weight — the unstable position requires good control.
Targets the gluteus medius for upper glute development
Stretches and stresses the adductors
Builds single-leg stability
Trains hip control through the cross pattern
Different stimulus than standard lunges
Builds the “shelf” of the upper glute

musclesWorked: Gluteus maximus and medius (front leg, heavy)

description.en: The dumbbell decline hammer press combines a neutral (hammer) grip with a decline bench. The palms-facing-each-other grip reduces shoulder strain while the decline angle targets the lower pec fibers. The combination is shoulder-friendly and effective for lower chest development.

en: Set a bench to a decline angle and secure your feet on the foot pads.
Lie back with a dumbbell in each hand at chest level.
Position the dumbbells with palms facing each other (hammer grip).
Pull your shoulder blades back into the bench.
Press the dumbbells straight up while keeping the neutral grip.
Bring the dumbbells together at the top of the press.
Squeeze your chest and triceps at the lockout.
Lower the dumbbells back to chest level with control.
Targets lower chest fibers on the decline
Neutral grip is shoulder-friendly
Reduces strain compared to pronated grip
Strong tricep engagement
Useful variation for lifters with shoulder issues
Builds chest size and lower pec definition

description.en: The dumbbell decline tricep extension performs lying tricep extensions on a decline bench. The decline angle keeps constant tension on the triceps throughout the range and provides a different stimulus from flat bench extensions.

en: Set a decline bench to 15 to 30 degrees. Hook your feet under the pads.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at arms length above your chest.
Keep your upper arms vertical. Bend at the elbows to lower the dumbbells toward your forehead or past your head.
Lower until you feel a stretch in your triceps.
Extend your elbows to press back to lockout.
Squeeze your triceps at the top.
Keep elbows pointing up throughout — do not flare.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Constant tricep tension throughout range
Decline angle provides unique stimulus
Builds tricep size
Dumbbells allow unilateral loading
Easier on the wrists than barbell
Useful tricep hypertrophy exercise

description.en: The dumbbell glute dominant step up uses a high step (knee height or above) and a forward torso lean to maximize glute engagement during step ups. The forward lean and high step force the working glute to do most of the work, minimizing quad involvement. It is a strong choice for glute development.

en: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Stand facing a high box or step (knee height or higher).
Place your right foot fully on the box.
Lean your torso forward at about 45 degrees from vertical.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Drive through your right heel to step up onto the box.
Squeeze the right glute hard at the top.
Lower the left foot back to the floor with control. Switch sides after the set.
Glute-dominant step up pattern
High step maximizes glute engagement
Forward lean targets glutes over quads
Builds glute size and strength
Develops single-leg stability
Useful for glute specialization

description.en: The dumbbell Larsen press is a flat dumbbell bench press performed with your feet held up off the floor (typically straight up or knees bent in the air). Removing leg drive forces the chest, shoulders, and triceps to do all the work, building pure pressing strength and exposing weaknesses.

en: Sit on the end of a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand. Lie back, kicking the dumbbells up to chest level.
Lift both feet off the floor — extend them straight up or hold them at 90 degrees with knees bent.
Brace your core hard. Maintain back contact with the bench.
Press both dumbbells up over your chest with arms extended.
Lower the dumbbells under control to the sides of your chest.
Press back up by squeezing your chest and triceps.
Maintain feet-up position throughout — no cheating with leg drive.
Use lighter weight than your standard bench — Larsen presses are humbling.
Eliminates leg drive for pure pressing strength
Forces strict chest, shoulder, and tricep work
Builds raw bench pressing strength (no leg help)
Exposes weaknesses in pressing form
Trains core stability under pressing load
Works at home with dumbbells and a bench

description.en: The dumbbell one-arm Zottman preacher curl is a bicep and forearm exercise performed on a preacher bench with one arm. You curl with a supinated grip (palms up), then rotate to a pronated grip (palms down) at the top and lower with the reverse grip. This works the biceps on the way up and the brachioradialis on the way down.

en: Sit at a preacher bench. Place the back of your right upper arm flat on the pad.
Hold a dumbbell in your right hand with a supinated (palm-up) grip.
Curl the dumbbell up to your shoulder, squeezing your bicep.
At the top, rotate your wrist so your palm faces down (pronated grip).
Lower the dumbbell slowly with the pronated grip — this loads the brachioradialis and forearm extensors on the eccentric.
At the bottom, rotate your palm back to supinated and curl up again.
Complete reps on one arm, then switch.
Use lighter weight than standard preacher curls due to the weaker pronated lowering.
Trains biceps on the concentric and forearms on the eccentric
Builds both bicep and forearm size
Preacher pad ensures strict isolation
Excellent for arm development
Easy to load progressively
Two exercises in one movement

description.en: The dumbbell reverse bench press uses an underhand (supinated) grip throughout the press, which shifts emphasis to the upper chest fibers (clavicular head of the pectoralis major) and reduces lateral elbow stress. It is a useful variation for upper chest development without an incline bench.

en: Lie flat on a bench with feet planted firmly on the floor. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at chest level.
Rotate your wrists so your palms face toward your face — fully supinated grip (underhand).
Keep your elbows tucked roughly 30 to 45 degrees from your body, not flared wide.
Brace your core.
Press both dumbbells straight up by extending at the elbows.
Press until your arms are fully extended above your chest. Maintain the underhand grip throughout.
Lower the dumbbells under control to chest level.
Use moderate weight — the supinated grip is more demanding on the wrists.
Heavy upper chest emphasis
Reduces lateral elbow stress vs. standard grip
Builds the upper pec without an incline bench
Different stimulus than standard bench press
Engages biceps as secondary movers
Useful variation for chest day

description.en: The dumbbell side lunge (lateral lunge) is performed by stepping wide to one side and squatting onto that leg while keeping the other leg straight. With dumbbells held in each hand, it builds the adductors, glutes, and quads while developing lateral mobility. It is one of the best exercises for hip and inner-thigh strength.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Take a wide step out to the right. Toes pointing forward.
Sit your hips back and bend your right knee, lowering your hips down on the right side.
Keep your left leg completely straight. Both feet stay flat on the floor.
Lower until your right thigh is approximately parallel to the floor.
Drive through your right foot to push back to standing.
Repeat on the left side. Continue alternating sides.
Keep your chest up and back flat throughout.
Builds the adductors, glutes, and quads
Improves lateral mobility
Trains single-leg strength in the frontal plane
Carries over to lateral movement in sports
Easy to load progressively
Different stimulus than forward lunges

description.en: The dumbbell single-leg calf raise performs calf raises on one leg while holding a dumbbell for added load. Training one calf at a time doubles the demand per leg and exposes left-right calf imbalances.

en: Stand on a step with the ball of your right foot on the edge. Hold a dumbbell in your right hand.
Hold a wall or rack with your left hand for balance.
Tuck your left foot behind your right ankle.
Lower your right heel as far as possible for a full stretch.
Press through the ball of your foot to raise as high as possible.
Squeeze your calf at the top.
Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch legs.
Aim for 15 to 20 reps per leg.
Doubles the demand per calf
Exposes left-right imbalances
Easy to load progressively with one dumbbell
Full range with a step
No machine needed
Useful at-home calf exercise

description.en: The dumbbell W-press starts with dumbbells in a "W" shape at the shoulders (elbows at 90 degrees, palms forward, pulled back) and presses them overhead while maintaining the W pattern. It emphasizes the rear delts, mid traps, and posture muscles.

en: Stand tall with a light dumbbell in each hand.
Bring dumbbells to shoulder height with elbows at 90 degrees. Arms form a W shape — elbows wide, palms facing forward.
Pull your shoulder blades together. Chest up.
Press the dumbbells up slightly and slightly out to the sides.
Lock out overhead with arms nearly straight.
Lower back to the W position under control.
Maintain scapular retraction throughout.
Use light weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Emphasizes rear delts and posture muscles
Builds scapular retraction strength
Excellent posture exercise
Combines raise with press
Useful shoulder warm-up or accessory
Builds full shoulder girdle strength

description.en: The EZ barbell lying triceps extension (skull crusher) is a tricep isolation exercise performed lying on a flat bench with an EZ curl bar. The angled grip of the EZ bar reduces wrist and elbow strain compared to a straight barbell, making it the most popular and effective skull crusher variation. It builds all three heads of the triceps through a long range of motion.

en: Sit on the end of a flat bench with an EZ bar. Lie back and press the bar up over your chest with arms fully extended.
Grip the bar with a narrow overhand grip on the inner angled portions of the EZ bar.
Plant your feet firmly on the floor. Brace your core. Pull your shoulders down and back.
Keeping your upper arms pointing straight up, lower the bar toward your forehead by bending only at the elbows.
Lower until the bar reaches just above your forehead or slightly behind your head. Feel the stretch in your triceps.
Extend your arms back up to lockout by contracting your triceps. Keep your upper arms still throughout.
Do not fully lock your elbows — maintain slight tension at the top.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use moderate weight; form matters more than load.
Builds all three heads of the triceps through a long range of motion
The angled EZ bar grip is easier on the wrists and elbows
Loaded stretch position drives effective muscle growth
Allows heavier loading than dumbbell skull crushers
One of the most effective tricep mass builders
Easy to load progressively over time

musclesWorked: Triceps brachii (long, lateral, and medial heads)

description.en: The full planche is one of the most difficult bodyweight holds in calisthenics — holding your entire body horizontal with only your hands on the floor and arms fully extended. Legs are together and straight. It demands elite-level anterior deltoid, chest, and core strength, and typically takes years of dedicated training to achieve.

en: Master all planche progressions first: lean planche, frog/tuck planche, straddle planche.
Position your hands shoulder-width apart on the floor or parallettes. Turn fingers out to protect wrists.
Protract your shoulders hard (push the floor away). Lock your arms straight.
Lean forward until your feet leave the floor.
Extend both legs straight back, together, keeping them parallel to the floor.
Your body should be completely horizontal with only your hands touching the floor.
Hold for as long as possible. A 5-second hold is an elite achievement.
This is a multi-year goal for most athletes. Consistent progressive training is essential.
Elite-level bodyweight strength demonstration
Builds extraordinary shoulder and chest strength
Develops world-class core bracing
Impressive calisthenics skill
No equipment needed (parallettes recommended)
Ultimate horizontal pushing strength

description.en: The hang back bar stretch is performed by holding onto a fixed overhead bar with both hands and leaning the hips back. The hang opens the lats, shoulders, and chest in one position. It is a classic decompression stretch used by lifters and athletes to ease tight upper bodies after pulling and pressing work.

en: Stand facing a fixed overhead bar.
Reach up and grab the bar with both hands shoulder-width apart.
Use an overhand or neutral grip, whichever feels comfortable.
Step your feet back slightly under the bar.
Lean your hips back and let your arms straighten.
Allow your shoulders to stretch overhead and your chest to open.
Keep your feet planted and arms straight.
Hold the position and breathe deeply, then step forward to release.
Stretches the lats and shoulders
Opens the chest
Decompresses the spine
Useful after pulling or pressing training
Eases tight upper body

description.en: Happy Baby Pose (Ananda Balasana) is a gentle, restorative yoga pose where you lie on your back, grab the outsides of your feet, and pull your knees down toward your armpits. It decompresses the lower spine, deeply opens the hips, and stretches the inner thighs. It is one of the most calming poses in any yoga practice.

en: Lie flat on your back. Bend your knees and bring them toward your chest.
Reach up and grab the outsides of your feet with your hands. If you cannot reach your feet, hold your shins or use a yoga strap looped around your feet.
Open your knees wider than your torso and pull them gently down toward your armpits.
Keep your ankles directly above your knees so your shins are vertical.
Press your tailbone, sacrum, and lower back firmly into the floor.
Relax your shoulders and head onto the floor.
Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply into your belly. Gently rock side to side for added massage if desired.
Release by letting your feet down and hugging your knees to your chest.
Decompresses the lower spine
Deeply opens the hips and stretches the inner thighs
Calming and restorative
Relieves lower-back tension
Gentle enough for daily practice
Often used to end yoga classes for relaxation

description.en: The inverted row with bent knee between chairs is an at home back move that uses two chairs to support a horizontal pole. With knees bent and feet on the floor, it works for beginners building back strength.

en: Place a sturdy pole or broomstick across two chairs about shoulder width apart.
Test the setup by hanging cautiously to make sure it holds your weight.
Lie face up under the pole with the chest below the bar.
Reach up and grip the pole with hands shoulder width apart.
Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor.
Pull your chest up to the pole by driving the elbows back.
Squeeze the upper back at the top.
Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Builds back strength with only chairs and a pole needed.
Bent knee position makes it beginner friendly.
Trains horizontal pulling without weights.
Develops grip and core control.
Easy to scale by adjusting body angle.
Excellent at home substitute for cable rows.

description.en: The kettlebell alternating hang clean performs a hang clean and switches the bell to the opposite hand at the bottom of each rep. This builds bilateral proficiency, grip endurance, and cardio conditioning while practicing the clean on both sides.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold a kettlebell in your right hand at hip height.
Hinge at the hips, swinging the KB between your legs.
Explosively drive your hips forward. Clean the KB to the right front rack.
Lower the KB back down. As it swings between your legs, switch it to your left hand.
Clean the KB to the left front rack.
Continue alternating each rep.
Maintain control during the hand switch. Use a smooth, rhythmic tempo.
Aim for 10 to 20 total reps (5-10 per side).
Builds bilateral clean proficiency
Develops grip endurance from switching
Excellent conditioning exercise
Trains both sides equally
Improves coordination
Time-efficient full-body exercise

description.en: The L-sit is a foundational gymnastics hold where you support your bodyweight on your hands with your legs extended straight forward at 90 degrees, forming an "L" shape. It builds elite anterior core, hip flexor, and tricep strength. It is a benchmark calisthenics skill and the foundation for many advanced gymnastics moves.

en: Sit on the floor with legs extended straight in front. Place your hands flat on the floor next to your hips.
Press your hands into the floor and lift your butt and legs off the ground simultaneously.
Keep your legs straight and parallel to the floor — body forms an “L” shape.
Press through your shoulders. Lock out your arms. Keep your shoulders pulled down away from your ears.
Engage your quads to keep your legs straight and pointed.
Hold for 5 to 30 seconds. Breathe steadily.
Lower with control.
If full L-sit is too hard, regress: tucked L-sit (knees bent), single-leg L-sit, or floor-supported L-sit.
Builds elite anterior core strength
Develops hip flexor and quad strength
Strengthens triceps and shoulders isometrically
Foundational gymnastics skill
Progresses toward V-sit and advanced calisthenics
No equipment needed (or use parallettes)

description.en: The landmine front squat is a front squat variation performed with the end of a barbell anchored in a landmine attachment. You hold the loaded end of the bar at your chest and squat. The angled pull of the landmine eliminates the need for perfect front rack mobility while still loading the quads heavily.

en: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment. Load the free end with weight plates.
Stand facing the landmine end. Hold the loaded end of the bar at your chest with both hands cupped underneath.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out.
Brace your core. Lift your chest. Stand tall.
Sit your hips straight down with a perfectly upright torso.
Descend until your hip crease drops below your knees.
Drive straight up through your feet. Squeeze your glutes at the top.
The bar weight pulls you forward and down — the landmine angle keeps you upright.
Eliminates need for perfect front rack mobility
Forces upright torso position
Builds quad-dominant squatting
Joint-friendly alternative to barbell front squats
Easy to scale by adjusting weight
Works at home with a landmine attachment

description.en: The leg bench side bridge is a side plank variation with the top foot elevated on a bench. The elevated foot increases the load and adds difficulty to the move. It is a strong oblique builder.

en: Set up sideways to a flat bench.
Lie on the side with the bottom forearm on the floor.
Place the top foot up on the bench.
Stack the bottom foot on the floor.
Brace your core and keep the body straight.
Lift the hips up off the floor.
Squeeze the obliques and glutes hard at the top.
Hold for the working set then switch sides.
Loads the obliques
Strong side plank variation
Builds the core
Useful for core size
Trains the side abs

description.en: The lying leg cross lies on your back with legs raised slightly off the floor and alternately crosses one leg over the other in a scissor-cross pattern. It targets the lower abs, hip adductors, and hip flexors.

en: Lie on your back. Extend both legs straight, lifted a few inches off the floor.
Press your lower back into the floor.
Cross your right leg over your left leg.
Open them and cross your left leg over your right.
Continue alternating in a scissor-cross pattern.
Keep both legs straight and off the floor.
Move with control.
Aim for 15 to 20 crosses per set.
Targets the lower abs and adductors
Builds hip flexor endurance
No equipment needed
Engaging variation on leg raises
Develops coordination
Builds core endurance

description.en: The lying leg hip raise combines a lying leg raise with a hip curl (reverse crunch) at the top. You raise your legs to vertical, then curl your hips up to push your feet toward the ceiling. The hip curl at the top is what engages the lower abs beyond just hip flexion.

en: Lie on your back, arms at your sides. Legs extended on the floor.
Raise both legs up to vertical (90 degrees).
At the top, curl your hips up — push your feet toward the ceiling. This lifts your hips off the floor.
Lower your hips back down.
Lower your legs back to the floor under control.
That is one rep. The hip curl at the top is the key portion.
Maintain lower back contact with the floor during the leg raise phase.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Complete lower ab exercise combining leg raise and hip curl
The hip curl engages lower abs beyond just hip flexion
No equipment needed
Builds lower ab strength effectively
More complete than leg raises alone
Progressive from standard leg raises

description.en: The lever pistol squat uses a leverage machine or assistance setup to perform a single-leg pistol squat with support. The machine reduces the balance and mobility demands of a freestanding pistol squat, letting you build the strength and pattern with weights you can manage. It is a strong stepping stone to bodyweight pistols.

en: Set up the leverage squat machine with light or no plate load.
Position yourself under the shoulder pads with one foot on the platform.
Lift the other leg out in front of you, keeping it extended.
Brace your core and grip the handles for stability.
Lower into a single-leg squat by bending the working knee.
Keep the non-working leg extended forward throughout.
Continue down until your working thigh is parallel to the platform or deeper.
Drive up through your working heel to stand back to the starting position. Switch legs.
Builds single-leg strength with support
Stepping stone to bodyweight pistol squats
Reduces balance and mobility demands
Heavily loads quads and glutes
Corrects left-right imbalances
Useful for beginners working toward pistols

description.en: The lever standing calf raise uses a plate-loaded standing calf raise machine. The shoulder pads load weight onto the upper traps while the balls of the feet rest on a raised step. The setup allows heavy progressive overload with full range of motion through the calves.

en: Step into a lever standing calf raise machine.
Position the shoulder pads firmly on your upper traps.
Place the balls of your feet on the raised step with heels hanging off.
Stand tall with knees slightly bent.
Allow your heels to drop below the platform for a full stretch.
Brace your core.
Press up through the balls of your feet, lifting your heels as high as possible.
Squeeze the calves at the top, then lower the heels back down with control.
Heavy loading for calf size
Full range from a step
Builds calf strength and size
Plate-loaded for progressive overload
Strong calf isolation
Useful for calf specialization

description.en: The plyometric push-up (plyo push-up) is an explosive push-up variation where you push off the floor with enough force that your hands leave the ground at the top of each rep. Some lifters add a clap mid-air. The exercise builds upper-body explosive power, fast-twitch muscle fibers, and pressing strength simultaneously.

en: Get into a standard push-up position with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, body in a straight line from heels to head.
Brace your core hard and pull your shoulders down and back.
Lower your chest toward the floor under control by bending at the elbows.
Lower until your chest is just above the floor. Pause briefly.
Press up explosively with maximum force, generating enough power that your hands leave the floor at the top.
If you can, add a quick clap mid-air. Keep your body line straight throughout the airborne phase.
Land with soft, slightly bent elbows to absorb the impact. Immediately drop into the next descent.
Repeat for low reps (3 to 8 per set) — power exercises lose effectiveness when fatigued. Use longer rests between sets.
Builds explosive upper-body pressing power
Trains fast-twitch muscle fibers
Improves rate of force development
Carries over to athletic movements like pushing, throwing, and punching
No equipment needed — works anywhere
Excellent finisher for chest workouts

description.en: The prisoner squat is a bodyweight squat variation performed with both hands clasped behind your head and elbows wide. The hands-behind-head position eliminates the ability to use arms for balance, demanding tall posture, core engagement, and good upper-back stability throughout the squat.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out.
Clasp your hands behind your head, elbows pulled wide.
Keep your chest tall throughout. Pull elbows back to engage upper back.
Brace your core.
Sit your hips back and down into a squat.
Lower until your hip crease drops below your knees.
Drive through your full feet to stand. Squeeze your glutes at the top.
Maintain the elbows-wide, hands-behind-head position throughout. Repeat for 15 to 25 reps.
Demands tall, upright squat posture
Builds upper-back and core engagement
No equipment needed
Develops squat pattern
Easy to scale by adjusting tempo
Useful for warm-ups and conditioning

description.en: The prone Y-raise is performed lying face down on the floor or on an incline bench, lifting both arms up and out at roughly 45 degrees to form a Y shape with thumbs pointing up. It directly activates the lower trapezius, posterior deltoid, and serratus anterior — critical postural muscles.

en: Lie face down on the floor or on an incline bench (set at 30 to 45 degrees).
Extend both arms forward at a roughly 45-degree angle from your torso, forming a Y shape. Thumbs pointing up.
Brace your core. Keep your forehead on the floor or hovering just above.
Lift both arms straight up off the floor, leading with your thumbs.
Continue lifting until your arms are level with or slightly above your head.
Squeeze your lower traps and rear delts at the top. Hold for one to two seconds.
Lower under control back to the floor.
Use no weight or very light dumbbells (1 to 5 lbs). 10 to 15 reps per set.
Activates the lower traps directly
Builds postural muscles that resist forward rounding
Improves shoulder positioning for pressing and pulling
No equipment needed
Excellent warm-up before upper-body training
Useful rehab exercise

description.en: The raise single arm push up is a push up variation where one arm is raised out to the side at the top of each rep. The single-arm raise turns the move into a side plank rotation that builds anti-rotation core strength along with chest and triceps.

en: Get into a standard push up position with hands under shoulders.
Set your feet wider than shoulder-width for balance.
Brace your core and keep the body straight.
Lower your chest toward the floor by bending the elbows.
Press back up to the top with arms straight.
At the top, rotate the body and raise one arm out to the side.
Reach the arm up toward the ceiling in a side plank.
Plant the hand back down and repeat with the other arm.
Brutal anti-rotation challenge
Builds chest and core
Improves shoulder stability
Trains balance
Combo strength move
Useful for athletes

description.en: The resistance band rear delt row is a horizontal pulling exercise where you anchor a band at chest height and row both ends back with high elbows, targeting the rear deltoids and mid-traps. It is a portable, effective alternative to cable rear delt rows.

en: Anchor a resistance band at roughly chest height (door frame, pole, or rack).
Grip both ends of the band. Step back so the band is under tension with arms extended.
Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core.
Row the band toward your face by driving your elbows up and out to the sides.
At the peak, your elbows should be at or above shoulder height, hands at ear level.
Squeeze your rear delts and mid-traps hard. Hold one second.
Slowly extend forward under control.
Repeat for 15 to 25 reps per set.
Targets the rear delts and mid-traps
Highly portable — needs only a band and anchor
Improves shoulder health and posture
Easy to scale by changing band thickness
Useful warm-up before pressing
Joint-friendly

description.en: The roll ball external oblique is a self myofascial release drill for the side of the trunk. Pressing a ball into the obliques releases knots that limit rotation and side bending.

en: Lie on one side on the floor.
Place a massage ball under the side of the rib cage.
Brace the body on the bottom forearm.
Keep the upper body relaxed over the ball.
Roll the obliques slowly over the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Cover from the bottom rib to the hip.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the obliques.
Improves rotational mobility.
Reduces trunk tightness.
Useful for golfers.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The roll ball peroneus is a self myofascial release drill for the outer lower leg. Pressing a ball into the peroneals releases tightness that contributes to ankle instability and shin pain.

en: Lie on one side on the floor.
Place a massage ball under the outer lower leg.
Stack the legs or stagger them for balance.
Brace the body on the bottom forearm.
Keep the upper body relaxed.
Roll the outer lower leg slowly over the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Cover from knee to ankle then switch sides.
Releases the peroneals.
Improves ankle stability.
Reduces lower leg tightness.
Useful for runners.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The scapular pull-up is a pull-up activation drill where you hang from a pull-up bar and use only your shoulder blades to pull your body up about an inch — without bending your arms. It trains the scapular depression and retraction patterns essential for strict pull-ups, and is an excellent warm-up before pulling exercises.

en: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, arms fully extended.
Start in a “dead hang” — shoulders relaxed, body relaxed.
Without bending your arms, pull your shoulder blades down and back.
Your body should rise about 1 to 2 inches as your shoulders engage.
Hold for one to two seconds at the top. Squeeze your lats hard.
Slowly release back to the dead hang position.
Repeat for 5 to 10 reps per set.
Keep arms completely straight throughout — only the shoulder blades move.
Trains scapular depression and retraction
Builds the foundation for strict pull-ups
Activates the lats and lower traps
Excellent warm-up before pulling exercises
Useful for shoulder health and posture
Highly accessible — works for any level

description.en: The seated back squeeze is a basic scapular retraction drill performed seated. The lifter sits tall and pulls the shoulder blades back and together while opening the chest. The move activates the rhomboids and middle traps and is a key posture builder.

en: Sit tall on a bench or chair with feet flat on the floor.
Keep the chest up and the back upright.
Set the arms at the sides with elbows bent.
Brace your core lightly.
Pull the shoulder blades back and together.
Squeeze the upper back hard at the end range.
Hold the squeeze briefly.
Release back to the start with control.
Builds posture strength
Activates the upper back
No equipment needed
Useful warm-up move
Easy to add anywhere
Strong scap activator

description.en: The seated chin-up is the same as the seated pull-up but uses a supinated (underhand) grip, shifting more emphasis to the biceps. You sit on the floor under a low bar, grip it underhand, and pull yourself up with leg assistance.

en: Set a bar at about arm’s length above while seated. Sit under it with legs extended.
Grip the bar with an underhand (supinated) grip.
Pull yourself up. Your heels stay on the floor for assistance.
Pull until your chin is above or near the bar.
Lower under control.
The underhand grip shifts more work to the biceps.
Bend knees more for more assistance.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
More bicep emphasis than seated pull-up
Chin-up regression for beginners
Adjustable leg assistance
Builds pulling and bicep strength
Progresses toward chin-ups
Accessible starting point

description.en: The smith standing calf raise is performed standing on a small block or plate under a smith machine bar resting across the upper back. The balls of the feet press down on the block to lift the heels. The fixed bar path allows for very heavy calf loading with safety.

en: Position a small block or plate under the smith machine.
Step under the bar with the bar across your upper traps.
Place the balls of your feet on the block with heels hanging off.
Unrack the bar by twisting the safety hooks.
Brace your core and stand tall.
Press up onto your toes by lifting your heels as high as possible.
Squeeze the calves hard at the top.
Lower slowly to a deep calf stretch.
Allows heavy calf loading
Safe and stable setup
Full range of motion
Builds calf size
Strong hypertrophy move
Easy to learn

description.en: The snatch pull is an Olympic lifting accessory exercise that combines a snatch-grip deadlift with an explosive high pull at the top. You pull the barbell from the floor with a wide snatch grip and finish with an aggressive shrug and elbow pull — without catching it overhead.

en: Stand over the barbell with feet hip-width apart.
Grip the bar with a wide snatch grip (index fingers on the outer rings).
Drop your hips low. Chest up. Back flat.
Pull the bar from the floor by extending your legs.
As the bar passes your knees, explosively extend your hips, knees, and ankles.
At full extension, shrug your shoulders hard and pull the bar up with your elbows high.
The bar rises to about chest or upper-chest height.
Lower the bar back down. Aim for 3 to 5 reps per set.
Builds snatch pulling power without the catch
Develops explosive hip extension
Trains the second pull of the snatch
Useful Olympic lifting accessory
Allows heavier loading than full snatch
Builds trap and upper back strength

description.en: The split sprinter high lunge holds a tall split lunge position with the arms in a sprinter posture (one arm forward, one arm back). The pose mobilizes the hip flexors and trains sprint mechanics. It is a great drill for runners and athletes.

en: Step one foot forward into a long split lunge stance.
Set the front foot flat with knee tracking the toe.
Keep the back leg long with the back heel lifted.
Stand tall with chest up and core braced.
Bring one arm forward and the other arm back, like a sprinter pose.
Sink into a tall lunge position with hips squared forward.
Hold the position and feel the hip flexor stretch on the back leg.
Switch sides and repeat with the opposite stance.
Mobilizes the hip flexors
Trains sprint posture
Useful for runners
No equipment required
Builds single-leg balance
Easy to add to any warm-up

description.en: The standing air bike (standing bicycle crunch) brings opposite elbow and knee together while standing, alternating sides rapidly. It targets the obliques and rectus abdominis from a standing position while providing cardiovascular conditioning.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hands behind your head.
Lift your right knee while crunching your left elbow toward it.
Touch or bring them as close as possible.
Return to standing.
Lift your left knee while crunching your right elbow toward it.
Continue alternating at a brisk pace.
Rotate your torso with each crunch.
Aim for 15 to 25 reps total or work for time.
Standing oblique and ab exercise
Cardiovascular conditioning
No equipment needed
No floor space needed
Engaging and dynamic
Builds coordination

description.en: The standing calf raise circle is a calf raise variation where the lifter rises up onto the toes and rotates the ankles in a slow circle at the top. The motion loads the calves through a wider range and works the small ankle stabilizers at the same time.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Press up onto the balls of both feet.
Hold the high position with weight balanced on the toes.
Slowly rotate both ankles in a circular motion outward.
Continue circling for several rotations at the top.
Reverse direction and circle the ankles inward.
Lower the heels back to the floor with control.
Builds calf strength
Trains ankle mobility
Improves balance
No equipment needed
Useful warm-up move
Hits the small ankle stabilizers

description.en: The standing hamstring and calf stretch with strap is a standing stretch done with a yoga strap or band looped around one foot. Pulling the leg up while keeping the knee straight stretches both the hamstring and calf together.

en: Stand tall with one foot planted on the floor.
Loop a strap around the ball of the working foot.
Hold both ends of the strap with one hand.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Lift the working leg straight up in front.
Pull the foot up toward the body using the strap.
Keep the working knee straight throughout.
Hold for the desired duration then switch sides.
Stretches the hamstring.
Stretches the calf at the same time.
Strap allows for a deeper stretch.
Useful for runners.
Improves leg flexibility.

description.en: The standing low body rotation is a trunk mobility drill that rotates the lower body while keeping the upper body still. The mover keeps the chest forward and twists the hips. It is useful for spinal and hip mobility.

en: Stand with the feet shoulder width apart.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Cross the arms over the chest.
Keep the shoulders facing forward.
Rotate the hips and pelvis to one side.
Pivot on the back foot as needed.
Return through center to the other side.
Continue alternating sides.
Mobilizes the trunk
Strong warm-up drill
Useful before training
Builds rotational range
Trains the obliques

description.en: Eagle Pose (Garudasana) is a standing yoga balance pose where you wrap one leg around the other and one arm around the other while standing on a single bent leg. It builds balance, single-leg strength, and stretches the upper back, shoulders, and outer hips. It is one of the most recognizable balance poses in yoga.

en: Stand tall. Bend both knees slightly and shift your weight to your right leg.
Lift your left leg and cross it over your right thigh. If possible, hook your left foot behind your right calf.
Extend both arms forward at shoulder height.
Cross your right arm over your left at the elbows.
Bend both elbows and bring your palms together (or backs of hands together if palms do not reach).
Lift your elbows to shoulder height. Press your palms together.
Sit your hips back as if sitting in a chair. Brace your core.
Hold for 5 to 8 breaths. Switch sides.
Builds single-leg balance and stability
Strengthens the standing leg
Stretches the upper back, shoulders, and outer hips
Improves focus and concentration
Develops body awareness
No equipment needed

description.en: Wall walks are a CrossFit/gymnastics movement where you start in a push-up position with feet against a wall, then walk your hands toward the wall while walking your feet up the wall — ending in a handstand position with chest near the wall. They build inversion confidence, shoulder strength, and full-body control.

en: Start in a push-up position with your feet flat against a wall behind you.
Place one foot on the wall, then the other. You should be in a high plank with feet on the wall.
Begin walking your hands backward toward the wall while simultaneously walking your feet up the wall.
Continue until your chest is near the wall and your body is roughly vertical (a handstand against the wall).
Hold briefly at the top.
Reverse the movement: walk your hands away from the wall while walking your feet down.
Return to the starting push-up position.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. This is challenging — start with 3 to 5 reps.
Builds inversion confidence
Develops tremendous shoulder strength and stability
Trains the core in inverted positions
Foundation for handstand work
CrossFit benchmark movement
No equipment needed beyond a wall

description.en: The weighted lying twist is performed lying with your upper back on a stability ball, feet on the floor, and hips bridged up. You hold a weight plate or dumbbell with arms extended straight up and rotate your torso side to side. The ball surface and bridge position combine to heavily challenge the obliques and core stabilizers.

en: Sit on a stability ball. Walk your feet forward and roll down until your upper back and shoulders rest on the ball.
Bridge your hips up so your body is straight from knees to shoulders.
Hold a weight plate or dumbbell with both hands, arms extended straight up above your chest.
Rotate your torso to the right, rolling onto your right shoulder on the ball.
Continue rotating until your arms point to the right side.
Rotate back through center and to the left.
Continue alternating for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Maintain the bridge throughout. Use moderate weight.
Loaded oblique rotation on an unstable surface
Bridge position engages the glutes and hamstrings
Develops rotational core strength
Ball surface adds instability
Excellent full-body core exercise
Easy to scale with weight

description.en: The weighted seated supination is a forearm builder that trains wrist rotation. The lifter sits with the forearm braced on a bench and holds a dumbbell at one end. The wrist rotates from palm down to palm up loading the forearm supinators.

en: Sit on a bench with the forearm braced flat on the thigh or bench.
Hold a dumbbell by one end so it sits vertically.
Let the wrist hang off the edge with palm facing down.
Keep the forearm flat throughout.
Rotate the wrist to turn the palm up toward the ceiling.
Squeeze the forearm hard at the top.
Rotate the wrist back to palm down with control.
Complete reps and switch hands.
Strong forearm builder
Trains wrist supination
Useful for grip strength
Builds the biceps brachialis
Strong arm wrestling carryover
Easy to scale
